name: Halo laser (hybrid fractional)

chain: Even tone, smoother scars and texture
angle.text: Halo combines ablative and non-ablative wavelengths in one pass and is used for sun damage, scars and pigment. Cited evidence is limited to small registered studies.

summary: A hybrid ablative/non-ablative fractional laser for photoaging and scars; only small registered studies are cited.
note: Thin sourcing; trial results not summarised.
currentQuick:
Halo is a hybrid fractional laser used in clinics for skin texture, tone, photoaging and scarring, combining two laser modes in one treatment.
Only small trials are registered.
How it works: Hybrid fractional systems deliver both ablative and non-ablative microscopic columns of laser injury to prompt skin remodeling.
Risks and caveats: Hyperpigmentation after laser treatment is a studied concern, particularly in darker skin tones [3]. Downtime depends on settings and is not detailed in the sources used here.
deepLead:
Halo is a hybrid fractional laser, a category that combines an ablative and a non-ablative fractional wavelength in a single pass, aimed at photoaging, scars and pigment. Source material for this entry is thin, consisting of clinical trial registrations that name the Profile Halo mixed fractional laser or hybrid fractional lasers generally .
Registered studies are small: a 15-person study of facial and neck photoaging with the Profile Halo , a 34-person study of various skin conditions including dyschromia and photodamage , and a trial of a hybrid fractional laser for acne scars in skin of color .

name: Fractional CO2 laser (CO2RE, Ultrapulse, SmartXide)

chain: Smoother scars and fewer deep wrinkles
angle.text: Fractional CO2 is the stronger laser option used for scars and deep wrinkles, with the skin renewing over a longer recovery. It is the best-studied of the fractional lasers; CO2RE, UltraPulse and SmartXide are common systems.

summary: The heavy-duty fractional laser for scars and deep wrinkles: best-studied, more downtime and risk than gentle lasers.
note: Higher risk of pigment loss and scarring than erbium lasers.
currentQuick:
Fractional CO2 lasers vaporize tiny columns of skin to resurface scars, wrinkles and photodamage. They are among the more intensive options in laser resurfacing.
Published support includes cohort studies and randomized trials, mainly for scars.
How it works: The 10,600 nm beam is absorbed by water in tissue, ablating microscopic channels and triggering collagen remodeling; untreated skin between channels speeds healing.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include hypopigmentation, hyperpigmentation, scarring, acne and herpes outbreaks [6]. Recovery is typically longer than for non-ablative lasers.
deepLead:
Fractional CO2 laser resurfacing uses a 10,600 nm carbon dioxide laser, invented by C. Kumar N. Patel at Bell Labs in 1964 , in a fractional pattern that vaporizes microscopic columns of skin while leaving tissue between them intact. Commercial systems include CO2RE, UltraPulse and SmartXide.
It is used in dermatology for acne scars, wrinkles, burn and surgical scars, and other conditions; published studies include burn-scar cohorts, acne scar studies in Asian patients and randomized trials combined with other therapies . Wikipedia notes that CO2 resurfacing carries higher risk of hypopigmentation and scarring than erbium lasers . The same device class has also been studied for vaginal atrophy, outside the appearance focus of this wiki .

name: Erbium YAG resurfacing

chain: Skin heals with less heat damage
Smoother texture, fewer scars and wrinkles
angle.text: Er:YAG resurfacing is used on acne scars, deep wrinkles and melasma, and is described as a shallower option with less heat than CO2. The skin-specific evidence in the sources is thin.

summary: A shallower, water-targeting resurfacing laser with less heat than CO2; skin evidence in the sources is thin.
note: Much published Er:YAG research is dental, not cosmetic.
currentQuick:
Er:YAG resurfacing shaves away thin layers of skin with a 2940 nm laser for scars, wrinkles and pigment. It is considered a gentler-heat alternative to CO2.
The cited research is largely dental or small skin registrations.
How it works: The 2940 nm beam is absorbed by water in tissue, ablating shallow layers with limited surrounding heat.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks of laser resurfacing include scarring, pigment change, acne and herpes outbreaks [2].
deepLead:
Erbium:YAG (Er:YAG) resurfacing uses a 2940 nm laser, strongly absorbed by water, to remove thin layers of skin for acne scars, deep wrinkles and melasma . Wikipedia says Er:YAG lasers carry a lower risk of hypopigmentation and scarring than CO2 lasers because they produce less heat .
Much of the early Er:YAG research concerns dental hard tissue and periodontal use rather than skin, such as 1989 ablation-rate studies . Skin-specific trials in the sources are small registrations covering skin aging, acne scars with PRP, and cutaneous neurofibromas .

name: Pico Genesis / PicoSure Pro

chain: Skin remodels with fewer side effects
angle.text: Picosecond lasers such as PicoSure Pro are used for acne scars, pigmented spots and skin texture. Published datasets are small and the evidence is still developing.

summary: Picosecond laser treatments for scars, pigment and skin texture; small published datasets so far, with the evidence still limited.
note: Evidence for appearance use is mostly small, single-device studies; results vary by device and condition.
currentQuick:
PicoSure Pro is a picosecond 755 nm alexandrite laser made by Cynosure that dermatology clinics use for acne scars, pigmentation and tattoo work. "Pico Genesis" appears in appearance forums and clinic menus as a name for picosecond-style skin treatments.
Published research on the PicoSure Pro for appearance is limited. A small prospective study has looked at it combined with radiofrequency microneedling for atrophic acne scars, and a 23-person post-market usability trial has been registered.
How it works: Picosecond lasers deliver energy in trillionths of a second. Proponents describe this as acting through a mainly photomechanical rather than purely heat-based effect, and a diffractive lens array can be added to produce small zones of skin change for scars and texture.
Risks and caveats: Treatments are performed in clinics and are generally described as having short-lived redness and swelling; pigment changes are a recognised concern with laser treatments of skin, especially in darker skin types. Long-term comparative data are scarce.
deepLead:
PicoSure Pro is a picosecond laser system from Cynosure that emits light at 755 nm (an alexandrite laser) and can be fitted with a diffractive lens array. It is used in dermatology and aesthetic clinics for conditions such as atrophic acne scarring, wrinkles and pigmented lesions. 
"Pico Genesis" is a name used in clinic and forum discussion of picosecond skin treatments; this article treats it together with PicoSure Pro, the device for which published research and trial registrations could be found.
Published evidence for appearance outcomes is limited to small studies. A 2025 prospective single-center study evaluated the PicoSure Pro with a diffractive lens array combined with radiofrequency microneedling for facial atrophic acne scars , and a completed 23-participant post-market usability trial was registered for wrinkles, acne scars and benign pigmented lesions .

name: Ruby laser

angle.text: The ruby laser was historically used for hair removal, pigment and tattoos, and is now largely replaced by newer wavelengths. It is the first laser ever built, which is why it appears on the wiki.

summary: The first laser ever built, once used for tattoos, pigment and hair removal and now largely replaced by newer wavelengths.
note: Historically used on pale skin; darker skin types face higher pigment-change risk and newer lasers have mostly replaced it.
currentQuick:
The ruby laser emits deep-red light at 694.3 nm. It was the first working laser, built by Theodore Maiman in 1960, and was among the first lasers used in medicine, including for tattoos and, from the 1990s, hair removal.
For appearance it is now mostly a historical technology: Wikipedia states that alexandrite and Nd:YAG lasers have largely replaced it for hair removal. Q-switched ruby lasers have also been studied for sun-related pigment spots (lentigines).
How it works: Ruby light is absorbed by melanin, so pigmented hair follicles or pigment spots heat up selectively. Pulse length matters: studies of hair removal used pulses in the hundreds of microseconds to milliseconds, while Q-switched ruby uses nanosecond pulses for pigment and ink.
Risks and caveats: Because melanin in skin also absorbs 694 nm light, pigment changes and burns are recognised risks, especially in darker skin. Wikipedia lists ruby among lasers for paler skin types in hair removal.
deepLead:
The ruby laser is a solid-state laser using a synthetic ruby crystal that emits pulsed red light at 694.3 nm. Theodore Maiman built the first working laser, a ruby laser, at Hughes Research Laboratories on 16 May 1960. 
Ruby lasers were among the earliest lasers used in medicine, including for tattoo removal, and were later studied and marketed for hair removal and pigmented lesions.  According to Wikipedia, alexandrite and Nd:YAG lasers have largely replaced ruby for hair removal. 
Studies in the 1990s reported follicle damage and hair reduction with normal-mode ruby pulses , and registered trials examined Q-switched ruby treatment for solar lentigines .

name: Alexandrite laser hair removal

angle.text: Alexandrite lasers are used in clinics to reduce facial and body hair, mainly on lighter skin with dark hair. Hair reduction is established across the hair-removal literature; the result is a reduction rather than total removal.

summary: A 755 nm clinic laser for hair reduction, used mainly on lighter skin with dark hair; reduction, not total removal.
note: Hair reduction needs multiple sessions; light, grey or red hair responds poorly, and pigment changes are a recognised risk.
currentQuick:
Alexandrite lasers emit 755 nm light that melanin absorbs strongly, so they are used for dark hair. Clinics commonly use them for fast treatment of large areas on lighter skin tones.
Published comparisons find alexandrite among the more studied hair-removal lasers. Wikipedia describes a 2006 review that found roughly 67 to 72 percent reduction at six months across alexandrite, diode and IPL.
How it works: Selective photothermolysis: the light heats melanin in hair and follicle while skin is cooled, damaging actively growing follicles. Because only growing hairs respond, multiple sessions are typically scheduled.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include redness, swelling, acne flares, burns and hyper- or hypopigmentation. Lighter hair responds poorly. The FDA defines "permanent" reduction as long-term stable reduction, not guaranteed removal.
deepLead:
Alexandrite laser hair removal uses a 755 nm laser, absorbed by melanin, to reduce dark hair through selective photothermolysis. Wikipedia lists alexandrite among the standard hair-removal lasers alongside ruby, diode and Nd:YAG. 
The treatment works best on dark, coarse hair, and light, grey, red or fine hair respond poorly; multiple sessions are needed because lasers act on actively growing follicles. 
Alexandrite lasers also exist in picosecond and Q-switched forms used for tattoos and pigmented lesions, which are separate treatments.

name: Diode laser hair removal (LightSheer)

angle.text: Diode lasers such as LightSheer are the common clinic option for reducing facial and body hair, suited to pale to medium skin. Registered clinical trials exist for the brand.

summary: The common 800-810 nm clinic hair-removal laser; LightSheer is a widely used brand with registered clinical trials.
note: Reduction rather than guaranteed permanent removal; pigment changes are a recognised risk.
currentQuick:
Diode lasers emit near-infrared light around 800-810 nm that melanin absorbs, and are among the most common clinic hair-removal devices. LightSheer is a diode laser line, with registered trials of its handpieces for hair reduction.
Wikipedia notes a randomized trial where diode laser reduced hair by 69.2 percent at 12 months versus 52.7 percent for IPL.
How it works: Selective photothermolysis: light is absorbed by melanin in the hair, heating the follicle, while skin cooling protects the surface. Only growing follicles are affected, so sessions repeat every few weeks.
Risks and caveats: Short-term redness, swelling and pain are common; burns and pigment changes are possible. A 2006 review described by Wikipedia reported side effects in 28.9 percent for diode versus 9.5 percent for alexandrite.
deepLead:
Diode laser hair removal uses semiconductor lasers around 800 to 810 nm to reduce hair by heating melanin in the follicle. Wikipedia lists pulsed diode arrays (810 nm) as suited to pale to medium skin. 
LightSheer is a diode hair-removal system whose handpieces (such as LightSheer Duet HS and ET) have been the subject of registered clinical studies. 
Wikipedia describes a randomized trial in which diode laser produced 69.2 percent hair reduction at 12 months, versus 52.7 percent for IPL.

name: Nd:YAG laser hair removal

chain: Follicles heated with less surface absorption
angle.text: Nd:YAG is the hair-removal laser people with darker skin tones turn to for facial and body hair reduction. Its deeper wavelength is chosen to lessen absorption in surface melanin.

summary: The 1064 nm laser used for hair reduction on darker skin tones, with deeper penetration and less surface melanin absorption.
note: Reduction rather than guaranteed removal; usually more sessions on fine or light hair.
currentQuick:
Nd:YAG lasers emit infrared light at 1064 nm. Wikipedia lists this wavelength as the one for dark skin in hair removal, and a 2022 prospective study said alexandrite and Nd:YAG are the most effective options in lighter and darker skin phototypes respectively.
Studies of fluence and histology in the early 2000s examined millisecond Nd:YAG lasers for hair removal.
How it works: Selective photothermolysis: the longer wavelength is absorbed less by skin pigment and penetrates deeper, targeting hair-follicle melanin while sparing the surface better in darker skin.
Risks and caveats: Redness, swelling, pain, burns and pigment change are possible; the general risks Wikipedia lists for laser hair removal apply.
deepLead:
Nd:YAG laser hair removal uses a 1064 nm neodymium-doped yttrium aluminium garnet laser to reduce dark hair. Wikipedia lists it as the hair-removal laser for dark skin. 
Bell Laboratories first demonstrated Nd:YAG laser operation in 1964, and the laser is used in cosmetic medicine for hair removal and minor vascular defects. 
Published studies include fluence comparisons and histology from 2001 and a 2022 prospective study comparing traditional and "in motion" Nd:YAG techniques.

name: Soprano Ice laser

chain: Hair growth slows with lower pain
angle.text: The Soprano Ice is marketed as a more comfortable hair-removal laser, combining 755, 810 and 1064 nm in one device. Evidence includes one small study of the Platinum model in darker skin.

summary: A diode-type hair-removal system marketed as lower-pain; one small study of the triple-wavelength Platinum model in darker skin.
note: Little independent evidence on the pain claim was found.
currentQuick:
Soprano Ice is a hair-removal laser line from Alma Lasers. The Soprano Ice Platinum combines 755, 810 and 1064 nm wavelengths in one device.
One published study evaluated the triple-wavelength Platinum for hair reduction in skin types IV to V.
How it works: Like other hair-removal lasers it targets melanin in hair follicles by selective photothermolysis, with cooling to protect the skin. Combining wavelengths is described as an approach to treat a range of skin types.
Risks and caveats: General laser hair-removal risks apply: redness, swelling, burns and pigment changes. Specific data on pain reduction versus other devices were not found.
deepLead:
The Soprano Ice Platinum from Alma Lasers (Germany) is a hair-removal laser that emits a combination of three wavelengths, 755, 810 and 1064 nm, in a single device. 
A 2021 paper in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology reported on its efficacy and safety for hair reduction in Fitzpatrick skin types IV to V.  The study background notes that laser hair reduction is among the most common laser procedures in dermatology and that ruby, alexandrite, diode and Nd:YAG systems exist.

name: GentleMax Pro

angle.text: GentleMax Pro is a clinic laser used mainly for hair removal across skin tones, and in looksmaxxing circles it is discussed for facial hair reduction. Evidence comes from small studies plus general hair-removal data.

summary: Candela's alexandrite-plus-Nd:YAG clinic laser, mainly used for hair removal across skin tones; evidence is small studies and general hair-removal data.
note: Professional device; outcomes depend on skin and hair type and operator.
currentQuick:
GentleMax Pro is a Candela clinic laser that combines two wavelengths, alexandrite (755 nm) and Nd:YAG (1064 nm). It is mainly used for hair removal and also lists pigmented and vascular lesions.
Laser hair removal as a category has a track record in reference sources, though most people need many sessions and light or fine hair responds poorly. Studies naming this specific device are mostly small or retrospective.
How it works: The laser light is absorbed by pigment (melanin) in the hair and heats the follicle. Two wavelengths let clinics choose a setting suited to lighter or darker skin.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include redness, swelling, acne flares, colour changes, burns and, rarely, a delayed hives-like rash. It is a professional device and registry results for its trials are not summarised in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
GentleMax Pro is a clinic laser platform made by Candela that combines a 755-nm alexandrite laser with a 1064-nm Nd:YAG laser in one device. It is used by dermatology and aesthetic practices, most commonly for laser hair removal, and its listed study conditions also include pigmented lesions, vascular lesions and pseudofolliculitis barbae (razor bumps). In looksmaxxing culture it falls under the hardmaxx category of professional procedures, usually discussed in connection with facial hair reduction.
Laser hair removal works by selective photothermolysis: light absorbed by melanin in the hair heats and damages the follicle while sparing most surrounding skin. Reference sources describe alexandrite (755 nm) as used across skin types and Nd:YAG (1064 nm) as the option generally used on darker skin, which is the rationale for pairing the two wavelengths in one machine.
Published studies that name the device are mostly small clinical series and safety reports rather than large controlled trials. They include a retrospective review of its use on children after ear reconstruction, a large clinic review of an uncommon delayed hives-like reaction after alexandrite epilation, and registered manufacturer-sponsored evaluations.

name: Candela laser

angle.text: In looksmaxxing discussion "Candela laser" stands for a family of clinic lasers used for hair removal, pigment, redness and skin tightening, so users pick the device that matches their target concern. Evidence exists per device, not for the brand as a whole.

summary: Brand name for a family of clinic lasers (hair, tattoo, vascular, pigment); evidence exists per device, not for the brand as a whole.
note: Not the SI unit; platform-level entry with thin, device-specific evidence.
currentQuick:
Candela is a maker of aesthetic laser systems. In looksmaxxing talk the name stands for the clinic machines it sells, such as the GentleMax Pro and the PicoWay.
Studies are per device and mostly small, so there is no single verdict for the brand.
How it works: Different systems use different wavelengths: alexandrite and Nd:YAG for hair and pigment, pulsed dye for blood vessels, picosecond pulses for pigment and tattoos.
Risks and caveats: Risks depend on the device and skin type and can include redness, pigment changes and burns. These are professional devices.
deepLead:
Candela is the name of a manufacturer of aesthetic laser systems, and in looksmaxxing discussion "Candela laser" refers to the clinic platforms sold under that brand rather than a single machine. Registered studies name its products including the GentleMax Pro (alexandrite plus Nd:YAG), a 1064-nm Nd:YAG skin-tightening system, a pulsed-dye (595 nm) laser and the PicoWay picosecond system.
These platforms are used in clinics for hair reduction, tattoo removal, wrinkles, acne, pigmented lesions and vascular birthmarks such as port-wine stains, according to the conditions listed in registered evaluations. Evidence is spread across many device-specific studies and is not a single body of work. This entry is distinct from the SI unit of luminous intensity of the same name.

name: Lumecca IPL

angle.text: Users look to Lumecca for fading sun spots, freckles and facial redness to get a more even complexion. It is an intense pulsed light device rather than a laser, and supporting studies are small, though IPL is an established category.

summary: InMode's high-intensity IPL for facial pigment and redness; supporting studies are small and IPL itself is an established category.
note: Professional device; pigment changes are a listed IPL risk, especially on darker skin.
currentQuick:
Lumecca is an InMode intense pulsed light device used in clinics for brown spots and facial redness. IPL uses broad-spectrum flashes rather than a single laser wavelength.
Studies naming Lumecca are few and small, mostly in vessel response and rosacea.
How it works: Flashlamp light is absorbed by melanin or haemoglobin, heating pigment or small vessels, with surface cooling to protect skin.
Risks and caveats: IPL complications can include hyperpigmentation; photosensitising drugs and damaged skin are contraindications, and one manufacturer states IPL suits light to medium skin tones.
deepLead:
Lumecca is a high-intensity intense pulsed light (IPL) device made by InMode, used in clinics for facial pigment and redness. IPL is not a laser: a xenon flashlamp emits broad-spectrum, non-coherent light, and filters select which light-absorbing targets (melanin or haemoglobin) are heated.
Published research naming Lumecca is limited to small studies. A study of 38 volunteers used three Lumecca IPL sessions and measured the response of dilated facial blood vessels with quantitative methods, and a 20-patient study assessed erythema reduction in rosacea after polychromatic light treatments. A 2025 registered trial compares IPL, an anti-redness cosmetic and their combination in rosacea.

name: Sciton BBL / Moxi / Halo

angle.text: BBL, Moxi and Halo are Sciton treatments people combine for sun damage, pigment, redness, texture and scars, aiming at a fresher, more even complexion. Supporting studies are small.

summary: Sciton's IPL, 1927-nm fractional and hybrid fractional laser treatments for skin tone and texture; supporting studies are small.
note: Professional treatments; evidence is mostly small pilots.
currentQuick:
BBL, Moxi and Halo are three treatments run on Sciton platforms: broadband light, a light fractional 1927-nm laser and a deeper hybrid fractional laser. Clinics sometimes combine them for pigment, texture and photoaging.
Published work naming them is small, mostly pilot studies and trials with a few dozen participants.
How it works: BBL uses filtered flashlamp light on pigment and vessels. Moxi and Halo create tiny columns of controlled injury so skin remodels.
Risks and caveats: Listed concerns include pigment change after laser, healing time with deeper resurfacing, and that these are clinic-only procedures.
deepLead:
BBL, Moxi and Halo are treatments performed on laser and light platforms made by Sciton. BBL (BroadBand Light) is an intense pulsed light treatment, Moxi is a fractionated 1927-nm laser, and Halo is a dual-wavelength 2940/1470-nm hybrid fractional laser, as described by the titles of registered studies. They are used for photoaging, pigment, redness, texture and scars, and are sometimes combined in one session.
Evidence is a mix of small studies. A completed 15-person pilot combined BBL, Moxi and Halo for skin pigment, a split-face study compared IPL with pulsed dye laser for facial erythema, and a 2023 study examined fractionated 1927-nm laser for diffuse pigmentation and actinic changes. Many older Sciton papers concern erbium:YAG resurfacing.

name: Moxi laser

angle.text: Moxi is used by people seeking a lighter-downtime resurfacing option for pigmentation, sun damage and skin texture. Evidence for these appearance uses comes from small studies.

summary: Sciton's light fractional 1927-nm laser for pigment and sun damage; only small studies exist.
note: Thin evidence; clinic-only procedure.
currentQuick:
Moxi is a light fractional laser on the Sciton platform that works at 1927 nm. Clinics use it for brown spots, sun damage and texture.
Published studies are small, with 15 to 30 participants in the registered ones.
How it works: It treats a pattern of microscopic zones of skin, which are then replaced during healing, leaving skin between them intact.
Risks and caveats: Studies do not summarise adverse effects in the registry entries; pigment changes are a general concern with lasers, particularly in darker skin.
deepLead:
Moxi is a light fractional laser treatment from Sciton that uses a 1927-nm wavelength, as indicated by registered studies describing a fractionated 1927-nm laser and a trial combining BBL, Moxi (fractionated 1927) and Halo. It is used in clinics for pigmentation, sun damage and skin texture.
Published evidence is small. A 2023 study examined a fractionated 1927-nm laser for diffuse dyspigmentation and actinic changes, and two completed registered studies tested the wavelength for diffuse pigmentation (30 participants) and for hyperpigmentation in Fitzpatrick skin types V and VI (15 participants). Fractional lasers treat columns of skin and leave surrounding tissue intact, and are described as lighter than ablative resurfacing.

name: Excel V laser

angle.text: Users turn to Excel V to reduce facial redness, visible blood vessels and sun spots for a clearer, more even face. Supporting studies are small.

summary: Cutera's 532 nm plus 1064 nm clinic laser for redness, vessels and pigment; supporting studies are small.
note: Professional device; evidence is small studies.
currentQuick:
Excel V is a Cutera clinic laser with a green 532-nm and an infrared 1064-nm wavelength. It is used for redness, small vessels, port-wine stains and brown spots.
Studies naming it are small, often a handful to a couple of dozen patients.
How it works: Green light is absorbed by blood and pigment; the 1064-nm light reaches deeper vessels. Heat closes small vessels or breaks up pigment.
Risks and caveats: Adverse effects are not summarised in the registry entries reviewed; vascular lasers in general may cause bruising or pigment change. Clinic-only.
deepLead:
Excel V is a vascular and pigment laser made by Cutera. It combines a 532-nm green laser (KTP-type, frequency-doubled Nd:YAG) with a 1064-nm Nd:YAG, and is used in clinics for redness, visible blood vessels, port-wine stains and pigment such as lentigines.
Published studies are small. A prospective study in 5 adults used a short-pulse 532-nm Nd:YAG (Excel V) for port-wine stains, a randomised open-label study compared 532-nm KTP and 595-nm pulsed dye lasers for erythematous surgical scars, and registered Cutera studies include rosacea, lentigines on the hands and poikiloderma of Civatte.

name: Laser genesis

angle.text: Laser Genesis is promoted as a low-downtime facial treatment for tone, redness and fine texture. Published evidence for the appearance effect is very thin, mostly a small split-face trial.

summary: A gentle 1064-nm Nd:YAG laser facial treatment marketed for tone and redness; published appearance evidence is very thin.
note: Evidence specific to this brand consists of one eight-patient split-face trial and small registered studies.
currentQuick:
Laser Genesis is a brand name for a low-energy 1064-nm Nd:YAG laser treatment that clinics offer for skin tone, redness and fine lines, usually described as having little downtime.
Published research on it for appearance is sparse. One randomized split-face trial in eight people compared it with fractional radiofrequency, and other registered studies are small.
How it works: The infrared light passes through the surface and warms the dermis without removing the epidermis; providers say this prompts collagen remodeling and less visible redness.
Risks and caveats: Nd:YAG lasers at 1064 nm carry an eye-injury hazard because the beam is invisible. Cosmetic adverse-event rates for this specific treatment were not found in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Laser Genesis is the name of a non-ablative skin treatment that uses a long-pulsed 1064-nm neodymium-doped yttrium aluminium garnet (Nd:YAG) laser at low energy. It is marketed for improving skin tone, redness and fine texture and is often described as a gentle, low-downtime option. A split-face trial refers to it as the 1064-nm long-pulsed Nd:YAG laser known as Laser Genesis .
The Nd:YAG laser medium emits infrared light at 1064 nm, which is weakly absorbed by water-rich tissue and is used in medicine for hair removal, minor vascular lesions and other dermatologic applications .
Published evidence specific to Laser Genesis for appearance is small: one randomized split-face study compared it with grid fractional radiofrequency for periorbital wrinkles in eight patients , and several small registered studies of 1064-nm devices exist .

name: Vbeam Perfecta

angle.text: Users seek Vbeam for facial redness, broken capillaries, rosacea-related flushing and some scars to get a calmer, more even complexion. It is well established for vascular lesions; evidence for purely cosmetic redness is thinner.

summary: Candela's 595 nm pulsed dye laser, a clinic mainstay for redness and vascular lesions; cosmetic-only evidence is thin.
note: Evidence is strongest for medical vascular lesions; bruising is a common effect.
currentQuick:
Vbeam Perfecta is a pulsed dye laser from Candela used by dermatologists for port-wine stains, hemangiomas, broken capillaries and persistent facial redness.
Its research base is mainly medical vascular conditions. Studies of it for general appearance, such as photoaging, are small.
How it works: 595 nm light is absorbed by hemoglobin, heating and closing small vessels. A cryogen spray cools the skin surface during each pulse.
Risks and caveats: Bruising (purpura) and temporary redness or swelling are recognized effects; settings such as pulse stacking have been studied to reduce purpura.
deepLead:
Vbeam Perfecta is a pulsed dye laser (PDL) system made by Candela that emits yellow light at 595 nm, a wavelength absorbed by hemoglobin. It is used in dermatology for vascular lesions such as port-wine stains, hemangiomas, facial telangiectasias and rosacea-related redness, and some practices offer it for scars and general facial redness .
Pulsed dye lasers have long been treated in the medical literature as the standard approach for port-wine stains . Evidence for purely cosmetic uses, such as photoaging, is limited to small studies .

name: Morpheus8 Burst

angle.text: Burst mode is the deeper setting of Morpheus8, promoted for skin laxity, texture and mild fat remodeling around the lower face and neck. Little independent evidence exists for this setting specifically.

summary: The deeper Burst-mode RF microneedling setting of InMode's Morpheus8; little independent evidence exists for it specifically.
note: Evidence is thin and largely industry-linked.
currentQuick:
Morpheus8 Burst is the Burst-mode, deeper-reaching configuration of InMode's RF microneedling device, marketed for tightening skin and mild fat reduction.
Specific published research is minimal; one registered trial looked at multi-depth RF microneedling for cellulite.
How it works: Insulated needles penetrate the skin and release RF energy at chosen depths, heating tissue to prompt collagen remodeling.
Risks and caveats: Redness, swelling and pinpoint bleeding are common; burns, scarring, infection and pigment changes are described as rarer risks.
deepLead:
Morpheus8 Burst refers to the Burst mode and deeper attachments of the Morpheus8 radiofrequency (RF) microneedling system from InMode, which uses insulated microneedles to deliver bipolar RF energy into the dermis and subdermal tissue . It is marketed for skin laxity, texture and mild fat remodeling.
Published independent evidence specific to the Burst mode is minimal. The registered trial that applies to this entry tested multi-depth RF microneedling for cellulite .

name: Morpheus8 Body

angle.text: Morpheus8 Body is used on the abdomen, arms and thighs for skin laxity and texture, for instance after weight loss. Evidence is limited to practice reports and one small registered study.

summary: InMode's RF microneedling for larger body areas; evidence is limited to practice reports and one small registered study.
note: Independent long-term data are limited.
currentQuick:
Morpheus8 Body applies InMode's RF microneedling to the abdomen, arms, thighs and other areas, marketed for skin tightening and texture.
Supporting research is limited to surgeon practice descriptions and a small registered cellulite study.
How it works: Insulated needles deliver RF energy to the dermis and deeper tissue, which providers say prompts collagen remodeling.
Risks and caveats: Temporary redness and swelling are common; burns, scarring and infection are described as rarer risks.
deepLead:
Morpheus8 Body is the body-treatment version of InMode's Morpheus8 fractional radiofrequency (RF) microneedling system, used on areas such as the abdomen, arms and thighs for skin laxity and texture .
A 2024 plastic-surgery review lists Morpheus8 and Morpheus8 Body among RF-based minimally invasive tools used alongside surgical body contouring . A registered 48-person study examined RF microneedling for leg cellulite .

name: Fractora RF

angle.text: Fractora is the RF pin handpiece that preceded Morpheus8, used for skin laxity, acne scars and oil control. It has been studied in small, mostly early studies.

summary: InMode's fractional RF pin handpiece, the forerunner of Morpheus8, studied for laxity and acne scars in small, mostly early studies.
note: Evidence is small-scale and often combined with other RF devices.
currentQuick:
Fractora is a fractional radiofrequency handpiece from InMode, used in clinics for skin tightening and acne scars; Morpheus8 was modified from it.
Studies are small, including combination protocols with FaceTite and a sebum trial.
How it works: Arrays of pins deliver bipolar RF energy into the skin in a fractional pattern, heating tissue to prompt remodeling.
Risks and caveats: Redness, swelling and pinpoint bleeding are commonly reported for RF microneedling; Fractora-specific adverse data were limited in the sources.
deepLead:
Fractora is a fractional bipolar radiofrequency (RF) microneedling-type handpiece from InMode, the platform that was later modified into Morpheus8 . It delivers RF energy through arrays of pins into the skin and has been studied for skin laxity, acne scars and oil production .
Published work is mostly small prospective and retrospective studies, some combining Fractora with other RF treatments such as FaceTite.
